sentences.text: September's report is more specific: gasoline rose 9.1 percent in that one month and accounted for over half of the month's whole rise.

excerpt.text:
The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased 0.6 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in 
September after rising 0.4 percent in August, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Over the last 12 
months, the all items index increased 3.7 percent before seasonal adjustment.

The index for gasoline rose 9.1 percent in September, accounting for over half of the monthly all items increase. The 
energy index increased 5.2 percent over the month following a 2.1-percent increase in August. The shelter index rose 0.4 
percent in September after rising 0.3 percent in August. The index for food was unchanged in September, as the index for 
food away from home increased 0.2 percent and the index for food at home fell 0.1 percent. 

The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent in September, as it did in August. Indexes that increased 
over the month include recreation, used cars and trucks, education, airline fares, medical care, and apparel. Conversely, 
the index for communication was among the small number of major indexes that decreased in September.

The all items index rose 3.7 percent for the 12 months ending September, a larger increase than the 3.4-percent increase 
reported for the 12 months ending in August. The all items less food and energy index rose 2.6 percent over the year, 
following a 2.4-percent increase over the 12 months ending August. The energy index increased 20.4 percent for the 12 
months ending September. The food index increased 2.5 percent over the last year.

excerpt.text:
from equation (4) for each horizon, as described in Appendix C. We subtract this predicted effect from the
item's actual price change and aggregate across items. The tariff effect is the shaded area, with a cumulative
contribution of around 2.9 percentage points by the end of the sample (February 2026). This counterfactual
should be read with care. Like any regression with time fixed effects, our specifications identify the effect of
tariffs on a good's price relative to less-exposed goods; the common, economy-wide component is absorbed
by the date fixed effects and is not separately identified: the familiar missing-intercept problem. The
counterfactual therefore treats these relative price effects as absolute ones, and should be read as illustrative
of the magnitude of the tariff-induced price increases for the goods in our sample.

sentences.text: The people quoted here mostly weren't arguing about the numbers; they were arguing about the yardstick.
So when someone tells you inflation is high or low, ask: compared with what, and over which months?
And when you hear the rate is falling, check core, and remember that a slower rate still means prices that are climbing.
